summary:
Santa Cruz stands under Argentina's national framework on gender identity, and no provincial departure from that framework material enough to score separately has been sourced. The operating position for a visitor to the province is the national one.

Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and an 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. Activists interviewed in April 2025 report that the law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Two executive decrees of 5 February 2025 narrowed that framework. DNU 62/2025 amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions; Reuters reported the ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. DNU 61/2025 altered the sentencing statute governing the placement of trans detainees in prison. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province, and therefore bind Santa Cruz. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measures unconstitutional, argued that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth, and mounted a judicial challenge.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm. Argentine trans activists, including organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, told the Washington Blade in April 2025 that the community faces a chaotic and desperate situation.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020; the gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's permissive statutory baseline is considerable: Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012, and was described by the United Nations as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

The distance between that statutory position and current executive practice is the principal turbulence in the record. The February 2025 decrees were described by legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes as illegal and unconstitutional and as a setback for the rights of adolescents, who signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Administrative hostility forms part of the operating environment. Trans activists told the Washington Blade that President Milei eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, and that the quota is no longer being implemented.
localsOnly:
Residents of Santa Cruz face the same suspension of gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions for under-18s as the rest of the country under DNU 62/2025, with legal experts warning that abruptly ending adolescent treatment endangers trans youth.

The federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which sets aside 1% of public-sector posts for trans people, is reported by activists as no longer being implemented after the dismissal of trans hires and the elimination of the national ministry responsible for gender policy. The national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was abolished under the Milei government.

DNU 61/2025 rewrites the rules on where trans detainees are held while serving sentences, a change that governs prison placement for residents rather than visitors.

Registration of civil-society organisations drew a negative assessment in Outright International's March 2026 overview, which bears on how community groups operate locally.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the judicial challenge to DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 has been decided, and with what result, is unresolved in the source inventory, which records only that the decrees face challenge and that experts intend to seek intervention.

No Santa Cruz-specific sourcing was available on provincial police practice, provincial court handling of hate-crime complaints, local facilities, or the province's own anti-discrimination law and its enforcement; the assessment rests on the national record.

The 227 hate crimes recorded by the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio in 2025 are a national figure, and no provincial breakdown for Santa Cruz is sourced.

Which specific provisions underlie Outright International's negative assessments for gender recognition and civil-society registration, and what basis the March 2026 overview gives for its deterioration finding, are unresolved on the sources provided.
